entities.name: European Food Safety Authority
entities.label: Institution
entities.summary:
The European Food Safety Authority (EFSA), established on February 21, 2002, in Parma, Italy, serves as a cornerstone institution within the European Union's regulatory framework for food safety. This agency was created to ensure a high level of protection for human life and health, while also addressing the interests of consumers and promoting fair practices in the food trade across Europe. The establishment of EFSA was driven by increasing public concern regarding food safety crises, notably the BSE epidemic in the late 1990s, which underscored the need for a robust and independent scientific authority capable of providing credible risk assessments. 

EFSA's mandate encompasses a wide range of responsibilities, including the evaluation of food-related risks, the scientific assessment of food products, and the communication of risks to the public. The agency collaborates with various stakeholders, including national authorities, industry, and consumer organizations, to gather and disseminate knowledge on food safety issues. Significant achievements include the implementation of the rapid alert system for food and feed, which enhances the EU's ability to respond to food safety emergencies effectively. By 2021, EFSA had issued thousands of scientific opinions on food safety, shaping regulations and consumer protection measures across member states.

The legacy of EFSA is seen in its influence on food safety policies and practices not only within the EU but also globally, as many countries look to its guidelines as a model for their own food safety regimes. EFSA's work has led to increased consumer confidence in food products, as well as a more harmonized approach to food safety across Europe, which has fostered greater trade and cooperation among member states. The agency's establishment marked a significant shift towards a more science-based approach in food safety governance, paving the way for future regulatory frameworks.
